practices.name: Recollection of former lives (pubbenivāsānussati): orientation
practices.howto: In the early discourses this is the first of the three knowledges the Buddha describes on the night of his awakening (MN 4). The later manual, Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga (chapter XIII), presents it as a by-product of fully mastered concentration: only after the fourth jhāna is steady does a meditator turn the mind back, sitting by sitting, through the day, childhood and birth, and, the texts say, beyond. Both sources treat it as a side-effect of a calm, purified mind and as fuel for disenchantment with the round of birth and death, never as a goal or a sign of progress. Satsang gives orientation only. The groundwork anyone can do is the breath meditation and the reflection on the round in this course; the knowledge itself is traditionally developed under a teacher inside a long retreat.
practices.source_note: MN 4 (dhammatalks.org); Visuddhimagga XIII, tr. Ñāṇamoli, The Path of Purification (Access to Insight). Satsang summary in its own words.
contraindications: No results are promised. Memories that seem to surface in meditation can be imagination or old impressions; the tradition warns against clinging to them either way.
Not for anyone living with dissociation, psychosis or unresolved trauma: stay with grounding breath practice and speak to a qualified teacher or clinician.
Do not try regression techniques from a summary or a video.
